tylosaurus:enwiki:6.title: Tylosaurus (Later discoveries and other species, part 2)

facts.statement: The genus Tylosaurus was established by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1872.
facts.quote: authority: Marsh, 1872

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Tylosaurus is Macrosaurus proriger.
facts.quote: type_species: Macrosaurus proriger

facts.statement: Known species of Tylosaurus include T. proriger, T. nepaeolicus, T. ivoensis, T. iembeensis, T. kansasensis, and T. rex.
facts.quote: subdivision: T. proriger Cope, 1869 (type) T. nepaeolicus Cope, 1874 T. ivoensis Persson, 1963 T. iembeensis Antunes, 1964 T. kansasensis Everhart, 2005 T. rex Zietlow, Polcyn & Tykoski, 2026

facts.statement: The largest species, T. rex, is estimated to have reached over 13 meters in length and weighed nearly 8.4 tons.
facts.quote: The genus contains at least ten validly named species, the largest of which, T. rex, estimated to have reached over 13 m long and weighed nearly 8.4 t

facts.statement: Fossils of Tylosaurus have been found primarily around the North Atlantic Ocean, including in North America, Europe, and Africa.
facts.quote: Its fossils have been found primarily around North Atlantic Ocean including in North America, Europe, and Africa

facts.statement: Fossil evidence indicates Tylosaurus engaged in intraspecific combat and acted as an apex predator consuming fish, birds, sea turtles, plesiosaurs, and other mosasaurs.
facts.quote: Fossil evidence shows that Tylosaurus regularly engaged in intraspecific combat and consumed various prey as an apex predator of their ecosystem, including predatory fish, ornithuran birds, sea turtles, plesiosaurs and other mosasaurs

facts.statement: Tylosaurus possessed an endothermic metabolism, a trait unlike that of nearly all modern squamates.
facts.quote: It had an endothermic metabolism, which is unlike nearly all modern squamates

facts.statement: The earliest known Tylosaurus fossils likely date back to before the 1500s and were probably discovered by Native American peoples.
facts.quote: The earliest Tylosaurus fossils were likely discovered by various Native American peoples and may have been the source of much of their folklore, with the earliest known ones dating back to well before the arrival of European settlers, around the 1500s

facts.statement: In 1804, the Lewis and Clark Expedition found a fossil skeleton near the Missouri River that was identified as a 45-foot-long fish.
facts.quote: In 1804, the Lewis and Clark Expedition discovered a now-lost fossil skeleton alongside the Missouri River, which was identified as a 45 ft long fish

facts.statement: The type specimen of Tylosaurus was discovered in the late 1860s by Colonel John Butler Conyngham and Mr. Minor in the Niobrara Formation near Fort Hays, Kansas.
facts.quote: The type specimen was discovered in the late 1860s by U.S. Army colonel John Butler Conyngham and a certain Mr. Minor in a deposit of the Niobrara Formation located near Monument Rocks, close to the Union Pacific Railroad line at Fort Hays, Kansas

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope presented a preliminary description of the type specimen in 1869 after borrowing it from Louis Agassiz.
facts.quote: Cope borrowed the specimen from Agassiz and presented a preliminary description of it in 1869

facts.statement: In 1872, Othniel Charles Marsh erected the genus Rhinosaurus to separate the species from the European genus Liodon.
facts.quote: In 1872, Marsh argued that L. proriger is taxonomically distinct from the European genus and must be assigned a new one. For this, he erected the genus Rhinosaurus

facts.statement: The name Tylosaurus means "knob lizard" and refers to the genus's characteristic elongated rostrum.
facts.quote: This name means "knob lizard" in another reference to the elongated rostrum characteristic of the genus

facts.statement: Joseph Leidy first formally transferred the species to the genus Tylosaurus in 1873, as Marsh had not done so originally.
facts.quote: Marsh never formally transferred this Rhinosaurus species to Tylosaurus; this was first done in 1873 by Joseph Leidy

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope continued to use the genus Liodon for a second species, naming it L. nepaeolicus in 1874.
facts.quote: Cope's persistence can be seen in his 1874 description of another species which he named L. nepaeolicus

facts.statement: The type specimen of T. nepaeolicus was discovered by Benjamin Franklin Mudge near the Solomon River and is catalogued as AMNH 1565.
facts.quote: The type specimen of this species was discovered by Benjamin Franklin Mudge near the Solomon River, and consists of several cranial fragments and a dorsal vertebra now catalogued as AMNH 1565

facts.statement: The species L. nepaeolicus was formally transferred to the genus Tylosaurus in 1894 by John Campbell Merriam.
facts.quote: This species, whose specific epithet refers to Nepaholla, the Native American name for the Salomon River is formally transferred to the genus Tylosaurus in 1894 by John Campbell Merriam

facts.statement: In 2026, Zietlow, Everhart, and Polcyn redescribed the holotypes of T. proriger and T. nepaeolicus, revising their diagnoses 150 years after Cope's original descriptions.
facts.quote: In 2026, Amelia R. Zietlow, Michael J. Everhart, and Michael J. Polcyn redescribed the holotype specimens of T. proriger and T. nepaeolicus, 150 years after their original descriptions by Cope, revising the diagnoses of both species

facts.statement: Louis Dollo described Hainosaurus bernardi in 1885 based on a skeleton found in a phosphate quarry in the Ciply Basin of Mesvin, Belgium.
facts.quote: In 1885, Louis Dollo described the genus and species Hainosaurus bernardi from an almost complete but poorly preserved skeleton discovered in a phosphate quarry in the Ciply Basin of Mesvin, Belgium, since numbered as IRSNB R23.

facts.statement: The name Hainosaurus refers to the Haine river near the fossil's discovery site.
facts.quote: The genus name Hainosaurus means "lizard from the Haine", in reference to the eponymous river located nearby the Ciply Basin.

facts.statement: Elizabeth Nicholls described a second species of Hainosaurus in 1988 from a partial skeleton found in Manitoba, Canada.
facts.quote: In 1988, a second species historically pertained to Hainosaurus was described by Elizabeth Nicholls based on a partial skeleton catalogued as MT 2 and having been discovered in Manitoba, Canada.

facts.statement: Timon Bullard and Michael Caldwell moved the species to the genus Tylosaurus in 2010, renaming it T. pembinensis.
facts.quote: it was in a revision published in 2010 that the species was moved to Tylosaurus by Timon Bullard and Michael Caldwell, being then renamed as T. pembinensis.

facts.statement: Some authors argue that the genus Hainosaurus should remain distinct from Tylosaurus based on dental traits, despite the 2016 transfer of H. bernardi to Tylosaurus.
facts.quote: Although this new combination has been widely recognized since, some authors nevertheless suggest continuing to maintain the genus Hainosaurus as distinct, justified in particular on the basis of dental traits not detailed in the 2016 revision.

facts.statement: Armand Thevenin described a new mosasaurid in 1896 based on a partial skull found at Éclusier-Vaux in Somme, France.
facts.quote: In 1896, Armand Thevenin described a new mosasaurid on the basis of a partial skull discovered at Éclusier-Vaux, in Somme, France.

facts.statement: Johan Lindgren reassigned the species to Tylosaurus in 2005 because its dental characteristics were similar to other members of the genus.
facts.quote: In 2005, Lindgren moved this species to Tylosaurus, notably due to its dental characteristics being closer to other members of the genus.

facts.statement: Per Ove Persson identified a new mosasaurid in 1963 based on isolated teeth found in Ivö Klack, Sweden.
facts.quote: In 1963, Per Ove Persson identified a new mosasaurid on the basis of isolated teeth discovered in a deposit located in Ivö Klack, near Ivö Lake in the Kristianstad Basin in Scania, Sweden.

facts.statement: In 2002, Lindgren and Mikael Siverson reassigned the taxon to Tylosaurus and referred additional cranial and vertebral fossils from Ivö Klack to it.
facts.quote: When the taxon was significantly revised in a in 2002 study, being reassigned to Tylosaurus, Lindgren and Mikael Siverson referred additional fossils to this latter that had been discovered at Ivö Klack, including cranial and vertebral remains.

facts.statement: A 2008 discovery of Taniwhasaurus in Japan revived the hypothesis that T. ivoensis might belong to that genus, though authors consider this a topic for future study.
facts.quote: However, in 2008, Caldwell and colleagues reported the presence of Taniwhasaurus in northern Japan and reaffirmed the dental similarities with T. ivoensis. This discovery revived the hypothesis of a possible reassignment of the species to Taniwhasaurus, but the authors see this as a subject for another study.

facts.statement: Miguel Telles Antunes described the species Mosasaurus iembeensis in 1964 based on a partial skull found in the Itombe Formation near Iembe, Angola.
facts.quote: In 1964, Miguel Telles Antunes described the species Mosasaurus iembeensis from a partial skull excavated from the Itombe Formation near the town of Iembe (hence the name), Angola.

facts.statement: Lingham-Soliar renamed the species Mosasaurus iembeensis to Tylosaurus iembeensis in 1992 because its cranial features matched Tylosaurus rather than Mosasaurus.
facts.quote: In 1992, Lingham-Soliar argued that the cranial features were not consistent with those of Mosasaurus and were more characteristic of Tylosaurus, the species being renamed as T. iembeensis.

facts.statement: Michael J. Everhart described the species Tylosaurus kansasensis in 2005 using thirteen specimens from the Niobrara Formation of Kansas.
facts.quote: In 2005, Michael J. Everhart described the species T. kansasensis based on thirteen specimens recovered from the Niobrara Formation of Kansas.

facts.statement: The holotype of Tylosaurus kansasensis, catalogued as FHSM VP-2295, was discovered in 1968 in Ellis County and includes a complete skull and six cervical vertebrae.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen, catalogued as FHSM VP-2295, consists of a well-preserved complete skull associated with six cervical vertebrae that was discovered in 1968 in Ellis County.

facts.statement: Caldwell and Jiménez-Huidobro questioned the distinction between Tylosaurus kansasensis and T. nepaeolicus in 2013.
facts.quote: At the 2013 annual meeting of the Society of Vertebrate Paleontology, Caldwell and Jiménez-Huidobro presented an abstract questioning the distinction between T. kansasensis and T. nepaeolicus.

facts.statement: A 2016 study led by Caldwell interpreted Tylosaurus kansasensis as a juvenile form of T. nepaeolicus, treating it as a junior synonym.
facts.quote: This hypothesis was further developed in a 2016 study led by Caldwell, which interpreted T. kansasensis as a juvenile form of T. nepaeolicus, thereby treating the former as a junior synonym of the latter.

facts.statement: Robert F. Stewart and Jordan Mallon rejected the synonymy of T. kansasensis with T. nepaeolicus in 2018, arguing the differences do not match ontogenetic variation in T. proriger.
facts.quote: In 2018, Robert F. Stewart and Jordan Mallon also rejected this synonymy, arguing that the differences observed between T. kansasensis and T. nepaeolicus do not match the ontogenetic variation documented in T. proriger.

facts.statement: Amelia R. Zietlow renewed support for the hypothesis that T. kansasensis is a juvenile of T. nepaeolicus in 2020 using a cladistic analysis.
facts.quote: In 2020, Amelia R. Zietlow renewed support for Caldwell's hypothesis on the basis of a cladistic analysis incorporating ontograms.

facts.statement: Bullard described the species Tylosaurus saskatchewanensis in his 2006 Master of Science thesis based on a partial skeleton from the Bearpaw Formation.
facts.quote: In his 2006 Master of Science thesis, Bullard described the species T. saskatchewanensis from a partial skeleton catalogued as RSM P2588.1, known from the Bearpaw Formation.

facts.statement: The specimen of Tylosaurus saskatchewanensis nicknamed "Omācīw" was discovered in 1994 near Herbert Ferry at Lake Diefenbaker, Saskatchewan.
facts.quote: This specimen, nicknamed "Omācīw" (meaning "hunter" in Cree), was discovered in 1994 near Herbert Ferry, at the Lake Diefenbaker, Saskatchewan.

facts.statement: Bullard and Jiménez-Huidobro formally described Omācīw as a distinct species in 2018 after it was more fully prepared.
facts.quote: In 2018, Bullard co-authored a multi-author study led by Jiménez-Huidobro which formally described Omācīw, which by then was more fully prepared, and confirmed its identity as belonging to a distinct species.

facts.statement: Zietlow, Polcyn, and Tykoski suggested in 2026 that T. neumilleri and T. saskatchewanensis could be junior synonyms of T. pembinensis based on anatomical similarities.
facts.quote: The following year, Jiménez-Huidobro and Caldwell noted the strong anatomical similarities between the dubious species T. neumilleri, T. saskatchewanensis, and T. pembinensis, later leading Zietlow, Polcyn, and Ronald S. Tykoski to suggest in 2026 that the first two could represent junior synonyms of the latter.

facts.statement: Samuel Garvey described a Tylosaurus specimen catalogued as TMP 2014.011.0001 in his 2020 MS thesis, found in the Puskwaskau Formation in Alberta.
facts.quote: In his 2020 MS thesis, Samuel Garvey described a specimen of Tylosaurus catalogued as TMP 2014.011.0001, discovered in the Puskwaskau Formation in Alberta.

facts.statement: Zietlow, Polcyn, and Tykoski described the species Tylosaurus rex in 2026 based on specimens from Texas and Kansas previously assigned to T. proriger.
facts.quote: In 2026, Zietlow, Polcyn, and Tykoski described the species T. rex based on numerous more or less complete fossil specimens discovered in the fossil record of Texas and Kansas, which had previously been assigned to T. proriger.

facts.statement: The holotype of Tylosaurus rex, catalogued as PMNS 8029, was discovered in 1979 in Lake Ray Hubbard, east of Dallas.
facts.quote: The holotype consists of a partial skeleton preserving, among other remains, a complete skull catalogued as PMNS 8029, discovered in 1979 in Lake Ray Hubbard, a reservoir located east of Dallas.

facts.statement: The Tylosaurus rex holotype was informally nicknamed the "Heath mosasaur" after the city where it was discovered.
facts.quote: The specimen was long informally nicknamed as the "Heath mosasaur", after the eponymous city within whose boundaries it was discovered.

facts.statement: The locality of the Tylosaurus rex holotype indicates it originated from the Wolfe City Formation, though its exact stratigraphic position is uncertain.
facts.quote: Its exact stratigraphic position is uncertain, but its locality indicates that it originated from the Wolfe City Formation.

facts.statement: The specific name rex for Tylosaurus rex honors a 1967 letter by John T. Thurmond to Barnum Brown suggesting Texan specimens were distinct due to their gigantic size.
facts.quote: The specific name rex, meaning "king" in Latin, is an homage to a passage from a 1967 letter written by John T. Thurmond to Barnum Brown, in which he suggested that some Texan specimens of Tylosaurus might represent a distinct species because of their gigantic size.

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope visualized Tylosaurus proriger as an "excessively elongated reptile" in 1870 based on the arrangement of its caudal vertebrae.
facts.quote: When Cope described the holotype specimen of T. proriger in 1870, he visualized it as an "excessively elongated reptile", due the morphological arrangement of its caudal vertebrae.

facts.statement: Cope described the head of Tylosaurus as conical with eyes on top and a pelican-like jaw and throat to facilitate prey entry.
facts.quote: For him, the head of Tylosaurus would be conical in shape, with eyes on top, and having a jaw connected to a throat similar to that of a pelican, thus facilitating the entry of its prey.

facts.statement: Cope believed Tylosaurus had only front flippers and lacked rear flippers.
facts.quote: Still according to Cope, the animal would have had only the flippers located at the front of the body, those at the back being absent.

facts.statement: Cope depicted the tail of Tylosaurus as long and flat, used for eel-like locomotion.
facts.quote: The tail is seen as long and flat, used in eel-like locomotion.

facts.statement: Samuel Wendell Williston began the modern understanding of Tylosaurus anatomy in 1898 with a major revision of Kansas mosasaurs.
facts.quote: Modern understanding of the anatomy of Tylosaurus started as early as 1898 with the publication of a major revision of the Kansas mosasaurs by Samuel Wendell Williston.

facts.statement: Williston estimated the maximum length of Tylosaurus at approximately 11 meters, a value close to modern estimates.
facts.quote: Williston also estimated the maximum length of the animal at approximately 11 m, a value close to those still proposed today.

facts.statement: Williston's reconstruction of a straight vertebral column for Tylosaurus is considered broadly accurate by modern standards.
facts.quote: Although the vertebral column was reconstructed as straight rather than curved, this skeletal depiction is considered broadly accurate by modern standards.

facts.statement: Tylosaurus was a derived mosasaur with advanced evolutionary traits including a fully aquatic lifestyle.
facts.quote: Tylosaurus was a type of derived mosasaur, or a latecoming member with advanced evolutionary traits such as a fully aquatic lifestyle.

facts.statement: Tylosaurus had a streamlined body, an elongated tail with a downturned two-lobed fin, and two pairs of flippers.
facts.quote: As such, it had a streamlined body, an elongated tail ending with a downturn supporting a two-lobed fin, and two pairs of flippers.

facts.statement: Derived mosasaurs like Tylosaurus are now understood to be more similar in build to ichthyosaurs, marine crocodylomorphs, and archaeocete whales than to giant sea snakes, due to convergent evolution.
facts.quote: While in the past derived mosasaurs were depicted as akin to giant flippered sea snakes, it is now understood that they were more similar in build to other large marine vertebrates such as ichthyosaurs, marine crocodylomorphs, and archaeocete whales through convergent evolution.

facts.statement: The largest well-known specimen is a skeleton nicknamed "Bunker" (KUVP 5033) housed at the University of Kansas Natural History Museum.
facts.quote: The largest well-known specimen is a skeleton of T. rex from the University of Kansas Natural History Museum nicknamed "Bunker" (KUVP 5033).

facts.statement: In 2026, Zietlow and colleagues estimated the size of the "Bunker" specimen to be around 13.2 meters long.
facts.quote: In 2026, Zietlow and colleagues estimated its size around 13.2 m

facts.statement: The genus Tylosaurus exhibits Cope's rule, showing a general increase in body size over geologic time.
facts.quote: The genus exhibits Cope's rule, in which its body size has been observed to generally increase over geologic time.

facts.statement: Early North American Tylosaurus representatives from the Turonian and Coniacian (90-86 mya) typically measured 5-7 meters long and weighed between 200-500 kg.
facts.quote: In North America, the earliest representatives of Tylosaurus during the Turonian and Coniacian (90-86 mya), which included early T. nepaeolicus and its precursors, typically measured 5-7 m long and weighed between 200-500 kg.

facts.statement: During the Santonian (86-83 mya), T. nepaeolicus and T. proriger were around 8-9 meters long, with weight estimates ranging from 1100 kg to 2592 kg.
facts.quote: During the Santonian (86-83 mya), T. nepaeolicus and newly-appearing T. proriger were around 8-9 m long, and estimated to have weighed around 1100 kg by Everhart (2004), and 2592 kg by Formoso et al. (2026).

facts.statement: By the Early Campanian, the species T. rex attained lengths of 13-14 meters.
facts.quote: By the Early Campanian, the newly emerged T. rex attained lengths of 13-14 m.

facts.statement: Everhart speculated that extremely old Tylosaurus individuals could have reached an absolute maximum length of 20 meters due to continuous growth.
facts.quote: Everhart speculated that because mosasaurs continuously grew throughout their lifetime, it would have been possible for some extremely old Tylosaurus individuals to reach 20 m in absolute maximum length.

facts.statement: Recent estimates for the holotype of T. bernardi range from 11.6 m to 12.2 m, whereas historical estimates erroneously placed it between 15-17 m.
facts.quote: The most recent maximum size estimates for the holotype of T. bernardi are 12.2 m by Lindgren (2005) and 11.6 m by Zietlow et al. (2026); historically the species was erroneously estimated at even larger sizes of 15-17 m.

facts.statement: Zietlow et al. (2026) estimated T. gaudryi at 7.1 m, T. kansasensis at 2.9-7 m, and T. iembeensis at 5.5 m.
facts.quote: T. gaudryi, T. kansasensis and T. iembeensis have been estimated around 7.1 m, 2.9-7 m and 5.5 m respectively by Zietlow et al. (2026).

facts.statement: A mounted skeleton of T. pembinensis nicknamed "Bruce" measures 13.05 meters long and was awarded a Guinness World Record for "Largest mosasaur on display" in 2014.
facts.quote: A mounted skeleton of T. pembinensis, nicknamed "Bruce," at the Canadian Fossil Discovery Centre measures at 13.05 m long and was awarded a Guinness World Records for "Largest mosasaur on display" in 2014.

facts.statement: A reassessment by Bullard and Caldwell (2010) found that the vertebrae count for the "Bruce" skeleton was exaggerated.
facts.quote: However, the skeleton was assembled for display prior to Bullard and Caldwell (2010)'s reassessment that found the species' number of vertebrae to be exaggerated.

facts.statement: T. "borealis" is estimated to be 6.5-8 meters in total length.
facts.quote: T. "borealis" is estimated at 6.5-8 m in total length.

facts.statement: The largest known skull of Tylosaurus belongs to the "Bunker" specimen (KUVP 5033) and is estimated to be up to 1.63 meters long.
facts.quote: The largest known skull of Tylosaurus is T. rex KUVP 5033 (the "Bunker" specimen), estimated up to 1.63 m long.

facts.statement: Tylosaurus skulls were between 13% and 14% of the total skeleton length, depending on age and individual variation.
facts.quote: Depending on age and individual variation, Tylosaurus skulls were between 13 and 14% of the total skeleton length.

facts.statement: The Tylosaurus head was strongly conical with a snout proportionally longer than most mosasaurs, except Ectenosaurus.
facts.quote: The head was strongly conical and the snout proportionally longer than most mosasaurs, with the exception of Ectenosaurus.

facts.statement: The Tylosaurus snout is heavily built and supported by a broad, robust internarial bar.
facts.quote: The snout is heavily built, supported by a broad and robust internarial bar (comprising the posterodorsal process of the premaxilla, nasals, and anterior process of the frontal).

facts.statement: Tylosaurus is one of only two mosasaur genera with clearly documented nasal bones, the other being the holotype of Plotosaurus (though one bone is missing there).
facts.quote: Tylosaurus is one of the only mosasaurs in which the nasal bones are clearly documented; the other is the holotype of Plotosaurus, although one of the bones is missing.

facts.statement: The frontal bone in Tylosaurus usually possesses a low midline crest, most prominent in T. proriger and moderately developed in T. saskatchewanensis and T. bernardi.
facts.quote: The frontal bone in Tylosaurus usually, but not always, possesses a low midline crest. It is most prominent in T. proriger, and is moderately developed in T. saskatchewanensis and T. bernardi, extending onto the premaxilla in the latter.

facts.statement: In Tylosaurus, the L-shaped jugal bone forms the bottom of the orbit and features a distinctive posteroventral process at the junction of its rami.
facts.quote: The jugal forms the bottom of the orbit; in Tylosaurus, it is L-shaped and has a distinctive serif-like extension at the lower back corner of the junction between the horizontal and vertical rami (arms) called the posteroventral process.

facts.statement: The quadrate bone of Tylosaurus changes from a hook-like shape in immature individuals to a robust oval shape in adults across several species.
facts.quote: In lateral view, the quadrate resembles a hook in immature T. nepaeolicus and T. proriger individuals, but in adult forms for both species and in T. bernardi, T. pembinensis, and T. saskatchweanensis it takes on a robust oval-like shape.

facts.statement: The suprastapedial process likely served as the attachment point for muscles that opened the lower jaw.
facts.quote: The suprastapedial process is a hook-like extension of bone that curves posteroventrally from the apex of the shaft into an incomplete loop, and it likely served as the attachment point for the depressor mandibulae muscles that opened the lower jaw.

facts.statement: In T. pembinensis, the suprastapedial process turns medially at a 45-degree downward angle.
facts.quote: In T. pembinensis, it abruptly turns medially at a 45° downward angle.

facts.statement: The genus Tylosaurus was named by Marsh in 1872.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Marsh, 1872

facts.statement: Recognized species of Tylosaurus include T. proriger, T. nepaeolicus, T. pembinensis, T. rex, and T. saskatchewanensis.
facts.quote: subdivision: * T. proriger (Cope, 1869) (tipo) T. nepaeolicus T. pembinensis T. rex T. saskatchewanensis

facts.statement: Cope originally proposed the name Macrosaurus proriger for a fragmentary skull and thirteen vertebrae collected near Monument Rocks in western Kansas in 1868.
facts.quote: Originalmente, el nombre "Macrosaurus" proriger fue propuesto por Cope para un cráneo fragmentario y trece vértebras recolectadas cerca de Monument Rocks en el oeste de Kansas en 1868.

facts.statement: Marsh established the name Tylosaurus in 1872 to include original Harvard material and more complete specimens found in Kansas.
facts.quote: Marsh finalmente erigió el nombre Tylosaurus recién en 1872, para incluir el material original de Harvard así como también los especímenes más completos que fueron hallados en Kansas.

facts.statement: A T. proriger specimen recovered in 1911 by C. D. Bunker near Wallace, Kansas, is one of the largest Tylosaurus skeletons ever found.
facts.quote: Un espécimen de T. proriger, recuperado en 1911 por C. D. Bunker cerca de Wallace, Kansas es uno de los mayores esqueletos de Tylosaurus jamás hallados.

facts.statement: Charles H. Sternberg found a Tylosaurus with plesiosaurian remains in its stomach in 1918.
facts.quote: En 1918, Charles H. Sternberg halló un Tylosaurus con restos de un plesiosaurio en su estómago.

facts.statement: Information about important Tylosaurus specimens reported by C. H. Sternberg in 1922 was lost to science until 2001.
facts.quote: Aunque estos importantes especímenes fueron reportados brevemente por C. H. Sternberg (1922), la información se perdió para la ciencia hasta 2001.

facts.statement: The specimen with plesiosaurian remains was rediscovered and described by Everhart in 2004.
facts.quote: Este espécimen fue redescubierto y descrito por Everhart (2004a).

facts.statement: Tylosaurus fossils date to the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Cretácico Superior

facts.statement: T. proriger lived from the late Santonian to mid-Campanian in North America, including Kansas, Alabama, and Nebraska.
facts.quote: Tylosaurus proriger (Cope, 1869), del Santoniense tardío hasta mediados del Campaniense de América del Norte (Kansas, Alabama, Nebraska, etc.)

facts.statement: T. nepaeolicus lived during the Santonian in North America, specifically Kansas.
facts.quote: Tylosaurus nepaeolicus (Cope, 1874), del Santoniano de Norteamérica (Kansas)

facts.statement: T. haumuriensis lived from the early to mid-Campanian in New Zealand.
facts.quote: Tylosaurus haumuriensis (Hector, 1874; =Taniwhasaurus oweni), del Campaniano inferior hasta mediados del mismo de Nueva Zelanda

facts.statement: T. kansasensis lived during the late Coniacian in Kansas.
facts.quote: Tylosaurus kansasensis Everhart, 2005, del Coniaciense tardío de Kansas.

facts.statement: T. proriger was among the largest mosasaurs, with the largest specimens reaching lengths of 12.8 to 13.7 meters.
facts.quote: Tylosaurus proriger (y junto con Hainosaurus bernardi y Mosasaurus hoffmannii) estuvo entre los mayores de todos los mosasaurios, los especímenes más grandes que se han encontrado contaban con longitudes de 12.8 a 13.7 metros.

facts.statement: Tylosaurus has a distinctive elongated and cylindrical premaxilla that may have been used to ram and stun prey or in intraspecific combat.
facts.quote: Una característica distintiva de Tylosaurus es su alargado y cilíndrico premaxilar (el hocico) del cual toma su nombre y el cual pudo haber usado para embestir y aturdir a sus presas y también pudo haberlo usado en combates intraespecíficos.

facts.statement: Stomach contents indicate that T. proriger had a varied diet including fish, sharks, smaller mosasaurs, plesiosaurs, and flightless seabirds like Hesperornis.
facts.quote: Contenidos estomacales asociados con especímenes de Tylosaurus proriger indican que este feroz mosasaurio tenía una dieta variada, incluyendo peces, tiburones, mosasaurios menores, plesiosaurios y aves marinas no voladoras como Hesperornis.

facts.statement: Tylosaurus appears to have preferred shallow coastal waters in some environments like Alabama, while favoring deep offshore waters in others like western US Niobrara chalk.
facts.quote: En algunos paleoambientes, Tylosaurus parece haber preferido aguas someras, cercanas a las costas (como en la formación Eutaw y la formación Mooreville Chalk de Alabama), mientras favorecía aguas profundas muy alejadas de las costas en otros ambientes (como en la creta de Niobrara del oeste de EE. UU.).

facts.statement: It is debated which of the many named Tylosaurus species are taxonomically valid, with only a few currently recognized.
facts.quote: Aunque muchas especies de Tylosaurus han sido nombradas a través de los años, solo unas pocas han sido por ahora reconocidas por los científicos como taxonómicamente válidas.

facts.statement: The Talkeetna Mountains hadrosaurid has uncertain classification, though its remains likely settled in a bathyal or outer shelf environment that later became the Matanuska Formation of Alaska.
facts.quote: El hadrosaurio de Talkeetna Mountains fue un hadrosáurido de clasificación incierta cuyos restos parecen haber sido depositados en un ambiente batial o una plataforma externa que más tarde se volvería la formación Matanuska de Alaska.

facts.statement: The size, shape, and spacing of bite marks on a hadrosaurid skeleton resemble those of Tylosaurus proriger teeth.
facts.quote: El tamaño, forma y espacio sin embargo, se parecen mucho a los dientes de Tylosaurus proriger.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the bite marks likely occurred after the carcass was dragged into the sea, as earlier biting would have perforated the body and prevented gas accumulation needed for floating.
facts.quote: Es improbable que las aparentes marcas de mordidas hayan ocurrido antes de que el cadáver fuera arrastrado al mar, ya que ello habría perforado el cuerpo, evitando la acumulación de gases de distensión que permitieron que el cadáver estuviera a la deriva en el mar en primer lugar.

facts.statement: The distribution of bite marks corresponds inversely to the presence of meat on the animal's body, with lower limb bones showing the most damage due to less protective flesh.
facts.quote: La distribución de las marcas de mordida corresponden inversamente a la presencia de carne en el cuerpo del animal.
